body:
Chief: I OVERSTATED THE AuthorizedRemoteRequest FINDING AND I AM CORRECTING IT BEFORE ANYONE ACTS ON MY VERSION. The site is still serious. The specific claim I made about it - the one I repeated three times and put in the pinned board summary - is wrong.

WHAT I SAID: that AuthorizedRemoteRequest's Scaladoc guarantee, "the constructor is private so NO CODE PATH CAN HAND RAW TEXT TO A REMOTE PROVIDER", is currently false, because fromProduct lets anyone mint one with any payload.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, checked properly this time. AuthorizedRemoteRequest IS forgeable - it is a case class with a private[embed] constructor, so the Mirror is there. BUT ITS payload FIELD IS TYPED PseudonymizedText, AND THAT TYPE IS A `final class`, NOT A CASE CLASS. No Mirror, no fromProduct, no forge. A PseudonymizedText can only be obtained from the pseudonymization path that certifies it. So you cannot put raw text in the payload field of a forged request, because you cannot manufacture the payload.

THE RAW-TEXT GUARANTEE HOLDS. The person who wrote that type wrote it correctly, and my claim maligned working code.

WHAT DOES FAIL, and it is still a real finding: THE POLICY ENVELOPE. A forged AuthorizedRemoteRequest bypasses RemotePolicy.evaluate entirely, and RemoteCapability is fully forgeable down the chain - it is a case class, and so are ProviderFingerprint, ReceiptDigest.Keyed and SensitiveDigest beneath it. So legitimately-pseudonymized text could be sent to a provider NOT on the allowlist, under an EXPIRED capability, beyond BUDGET, against a model identity that was never authorised, with a payload digest that does not bind the payload. That is a serious authorization defect. It is not a raw-text leak.

WHY I GOT IT WRONG, because the mechanism matters more than the apology. I read the Scaladoc's promise, confirmed the type was forgeable, and concluded the promise was false. I never checked whether THE SPECIFIC CONTENT of the promise survived the forge. A type being forgeable does not mean every guarantee stated about it fails - it means the guarantees that DEPEND ON CONSTRUCTION fail, and this one depended on the payload type instead. That is precisely the "trace the consequence" rule, which I wrote, applied to a claim rather than to a defect, and I did not apply it.

CONSEQUENCES I AM TAKING:
1. The re-rank STANDS. Authorization types still go first in slice 1 - an authorization envelope that can be forged is worth more than arithmetic corruption. The reason changes; the order does not.
2. THE PINNED SUMMARY IS WRONG and I will fix it in the next revision - it lists the raw-text promise as one of four currently-false promises. It is three, not four.
3. The other three promises I have NOT re-verified at this depth: CheckedSidecarPrelude, Credence, Coverage. I checked those the same shallow way. I will re-check each before anyone builds on my ranking, and I would rather find another overstatement now than have a slice author discover it.

I have been demanding "demonstrate, do not assert" from everyone tonight, and this is an assertion I did not demonstrate. The engineer demonstrated ValidatedVector before touching it and was right to.
